| "At least 1 point or more of margin each year" | Q3'25, repeated Q4'25 | Net margin: 5.5% (2023) → 5.5% (2024) → 5.7% (2025). Roughly **flat**, not +1pt/yr. | **Not delivered.** Analyst Scott Group caught this in Q4 2025 — see §5. |
| "Free cash flow to expand and free cash flow conversion to expand both" | Q2'25 (Leskinen) | **Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow $2.54B, down 33% year over year.** | **Refuted so far.** The one forward claim the numbers actively contradict. |
| Premium/brand-loyal demand is recession-resilient | Q3'25, Q1'26 | Q1 2026 premium revenue +13.6%, premium unit revenue +8.9%, leading main cabin by 4 points. Q2 2026 premium revenue +16.4%, premium unit revenue +11.6%, Polaris/Premium Plus +13.6%. | **Corroborated across two shock quarters.** |
| "Tripled our cash balance… strengthened our balance sheet… highest credit rating in almost three decades" | Q1'26 | Cash and short-term investments **$16.64B** against borrowings of $26.46B plus $7.20B of capitalized leases — **net debt $17.03B** including leases, about $9.83B excluding them. **Altman-Z of 1.2** sits in the distress zone. | **True on liquidity, misleading on solvency.** The cash is real. The balance sheet is still an airline's. |
| Recovering 100% of the fuel increase | Q1'26 goal → Q2'26 result | Q2 2026: recovered **about half**. Pretax margin 4.8% against a **$2.3B year-over-year fuel headwind**. | **On track but behind.** Half in one quarter, against a target of all of it. |

**Where the story is richer than the numbers justify:** the word "irreversible." Nothing in a 4.3% return on invested capital is irreversible. Airlines have declared structural change before every cycle.

**Where the story is poorer than the numbers justify:** the pricing power. Q4 2026 yield is currently tracking **up 19% year over year**, with Q3 at the same point in the booking curve up only 5%. That is a far more concrete fact than anything in the prepared remarks, and management buried it in the Q2 2026 revenue section.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising — but the confidence has migrated from the present to the future.**

- **Q1 2025 — hedged.** "There's a reasonable chance that bookings could weaken from here." Two scenarios given. Defensive vocabulary: "diligent about expenses," "removing capacity."
- **Q2 2025 — recovering.** "Demand feels to us like it has inflected upward." Note the hedge: "It's only 3 weeks' worth of data."
- **Q3 2025 — peak offense.** "I'd bet that our multiples move up meaningfully as well." A chief executive betting on his own multiple is the highest-confidence sentence in the file.
- **Q4 2025 — assured but caught.** The tone is celebratory; then Leskinen gets pinned on arithmetic and retreats to "the timing of which there's some uncertainty around."
- **Q1 2026 — confident under fire.** Fuel doubles and the target does not die; it moves a year. "I feel very good about 100% recovery and getting to double-digit margins in 2027."
- **Q2 2026 — the most confident language in the file, on the least visible year.** "Our confidence in our ability to deliver double digit pretax margins by 2027 and mid-teen pretax margins beyond that has never been higher." And: "our multiples do not yet reflect it, we believe this industry has structurally changed."

**The pattern that matters:** as near-term visibility has fallen, the *stated* confidence has risen, and the confidence has been placed further out. In Q1 2025 they guided the current year with two scenarios. In Q2 2026 they guided the current quarter 17% below where the street sat, and simultaneously declared record confidence in a target 18 months away. That is not dishonest — but it is the classic shape of a management team asking to be judged on a year it cannot yet see.

**Offensive-to-defensive language:** genuinely reversed course. Defensive in Q1 2025, offensive from Q3 2025 onward, and — notably — it stayed offensive through the fuel shock. That is rare and counts for something.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: High.** This is the strongest section of the file, and it is the reason this name deserves a serious hearing rather than a dismissal.

| Guidance given | Delivered | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 2025: FY2025 recession-scenario floor of "$7 to $9 per share" | FY2025 adjusted earnings landed near **$10.66** | **Over-delivered**, and against the *downside* scenario |
| Q2 2025: "$2 billion of free cash flow this year" | Trailing free cash flow $2.54B | **Delivered** |
| Q2 2025: Newark to cost about 1.2 margin points in Q2, about 1 point in Q3, nothing in Q4 | Q3 2025 delivered a beat ($2.78 vs $2.65) | **Delivered, precisely quantified in advance** |
| Q4 2025: "the only U.S. airline that managed to grow EPS year-over-year" | EPS $9.45 (2024) → $10.22 (2025) | **Delivered** |
| Q2 2026 guide of $1 to $2 per share | **$1.99** — the high end | **Delivered** |
| Earnings beat rate | **8 of 8 quarters** (Q2 2026: $1.99 vs $1.91 estimated) | **100%** |

**Is there sandbagging?** Yes, and it is disclosed rather than concealed. Leskinen in Q4 2025, asked directly why the guide implied less than the promised point of margin: *"Scott, I love that you did the math. And trust me, we've done the math, too… The full year guide was very deliberate. We're telling you that if current booking trends stay on this path, there's upside."* That is an executive openly admitting the guide is set to be beaten. An eight-for-eight beat rate against deliberately-low bars is a management skill, not an earnings surprise.

**The credibility event of this quarter.** On 2026-07-16 United changed its guidance policy on fuel: *"we have decided to once again be a leader by changing our guidance policy on fuel. We feel we owe it to investors to update our practice and provide guidance to reflect the most current fuel prices."* The Q3 guide of $2.50–$3.50 is now struck at an all-in fuel price of about $3.69 a gallon "based on Tuesday's curve." This makes the guide **harder** to beat and it is why the Q3 number came in below the street's roughly $3.60. Management gave up its own sandbag. That is a genuine, and rare, pro-transparency act — and it deserves credit.

**The offsetting deduction.** The full-year guide was "raised" to $9–$11 from $7–$11. Only the floor moved; **the ceiling did not budge**. And the midpoint of $10 is roughly 6% *below* 2025's approximately $10.66. Headlines read "raises guidance." The arithmetic reads "narrows a range around a flat-to-down year." First-half 2026 earnings of $3.18 compare to about $4.78 a year ago — down a third.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The question management keeps not answering: where is the promised margin?**

Scott Group of Wolfe Research, Q4 2025, is the cleanest example: *"I would have thought this would have been the year where like it's a pretty clear like point of margin. Like is it just the conservatism…?"* Leskinen's answer opened with a compliment ("I love that you did the math") and closed on "the timing of which there's some uncertainty around." He never said when. Three quarters later the target has moved to 2027.

**The question that later turned into bad news.** Ravi Shanker, Q1 2025, asked whether the fuel assumption differed between the base and recession scenarios, probing whether a downturn would bring a fuel offset. Leskinen conceded the point: *"if revenue falls off as much as we downside scenario… there's a solid case to be made that we would see further decline in fuel."* The hedge ran the other way. Fuel doubled *without* a demand collapse — United got the bad half of the correlation and none of the offset. Twelve months later that is a $6B cost line.

**Where analysts keep pushing and management keeps deflecting:**
- **Capacity discipline.** Atul Maheswari (UBS, Q4 2025) asked how discipline survives Boeing and Airbus ramping deliveries. Kirby refused the premise outright — *"we never say those words and I'm not even going to repeat them"* — and redirected to engines as the true constraint. It is a good answer, but it is a redirect: he answered about the industry's ability to grow, not about United's willingness not to.
- **Free cash flow and peak capital spending.** Brandon Oglenski (Q2 2025) and Andrew Didora (Q2 2026) both asked when spending peaks. Neither got a year. Leskinen's Q2 2026 answer — *"We are focused on free cash flow, uniquely focused on free cash flow… a 50% conversion rate for the next few years, heading to 75% as we exit the decade"* — gives a ratio instead of a date, and then adds the escape hatch: *"As we get there faster, we may allow CapEx to be a little bit higher."* Free cash flow is a residual in this plan, not a commitment.
- **Consolidation.** Q1 2026: *"there's been a lot of press coverage regarding consolidation rumors. We've not commented specifically on those reports and aren't going to start today. So you can ask me about it if you'd like, but you won't be getting anything new from me on it today."* A pre-emptive refusal to discuss a topic nobody had raised yet is worth noting.

**What analysts worry about that management is not addressing: the elasticity that has not arrived.** Kirby said in Q1 2026 that raising yields 15–20% must reduce demand — *"While we haven't actually seen that decline yet, ECON 101 makes us believe it's coming."* Two quarters later, United is setting passenger records at higher fares and the decline still has not come. Management has not revisited its own prediction. Either the brand-loyalty thesis is right and the textbook is wrong for this franchise, or the elasticity is simply lagged and lands in a quarter nobody has modelled. Nobody on the call made management pick.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Return on invested capital of 4.3% under a "we have won" narrative.** Six quarters of triumphalism sit on top of returns below any plausible cost of capital. This is the central contradiction of the file.

🔴 **Free cash flow down 33% year over year to $2.54B**, directly against Leskinen's Q2 2025 promise that "free cash flow to expand and free cash flow conversion to expand both." The one testable forward claim, and it has gone the wrong way.

🔴 **Insider behaviour contradicts the language.** Zero open-market purchases against five sales totalling 96,381 shares. Management that believes its own "our multiples do not yet reflect it" (Q2 2026) is not buying the multiple.

🔴 **Altman-Z of 1.2** — a distress-zone solvency reading — carried into a doubled-fuel environment with peak capital spending still ahead.

🔴 **The margin promise has been restated three times and delivered zero times.** "At least 1 point a year" (Q3 2025) produced flat margins; double-digit "next year" (Q1 2026) means 2027; each restatement arrives with more confidence than the last.

🔴 **The single-factor exposure is total.** Everything — the 2027 target, the guide, the multiple — resolves on the price of one commodity United does not control. Brent crude is $84.82 today against about $71 sixteen days ago.

🟢 **Eight consecutive earnings beats**, including through a fuel shock that doubled a quarter of the cost base.

🟢 **The Newark outcome is a durable, awarded advantage.** Management turned a reputational disaster into FAA hourly flight caps at its own hub — a regulatory-license benefit competitors cannot copy or lobby away easily. Toby Enqvist, Q2 2025: *"it's likely we'll look back and find that this long-term capacity fix is the most important and positive outcome."* That is the rare case where the spin is probably true.

🟢 **The loyalty flywheel is corroborated by hard numbers, not adjectives** — record second-quarter co-brand account growth of 22%, card spend up 14%, enrollments outpacing capacity by 5 points, all during a fare shock.

🟢 **The fuel guidance-policy change (2026-07-16)** removes management's own sandbag and marks guidance to the live curve. It cost them a Q3 headline and it is the most credibility-positive act in the file.

🟢 **Pricing power is demonstrated, not asserted.** Q4 yield tracking up 19% year over year; recovering half the fuel increase inside a single quarter.

🟢 **Competitive structure is genuinely improving.** Spirit's failure, low-cost carriers retreating from expensive hubs, and Nocella's Q3 2025 read that "unprofitable capacity is leaving the system" are corroborated by external events, not just management framing.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**"Structural, permanent and irreversible" has hardened from an argument into a liturgy.** In Q1 2025 Kirby *defended* the claim with evidence — brand-loyal leadership in six of seven hubs, the Southwest historical analogy, the spill-airline mechanic. By Q1 2026 it is recited in the opening paragraph as a given. When a management team stops arguing for its central claim and starts assuming it, the claim has become identity rather than analysis.

**The most revealing sentence in six quarters is about the multiple, not the business.** Q3 2025: *"I'd bet that our multiples move up meaningfully as well."* Q2 2026: *"our multiples do not yet reflect it."* Kirby is no longer only running an airline; he is arguing a valuation. Chief executives make that argument when they believe the operating case is already made and the market disagrees. It is also the argument that is hardest to deliver, because it is the one thing entirely outside his control.

**A quiet shift from "capacity" to "yield management."** Q2 2026: *"The capacity side of the equation is really yield management. You know, how often you sell the lowest fare versus higher fares."* United is redefining capacity discipline as a pricing decision rather than a fleet decision — which is convenient, because the fleet is growing about 8% and cannot be undone.

**Cost inflation is being reframed as an industry-wide shared burden.** Q2 2026: *"the cost structure inflation and the harmonies that mean everyone's costs have gone up. On those things that are outside of our control… it is 90% of the driver."* This is the groundwork for arguing that fares must rise industry-wide — a thesis that depends on competitors behaving, which is the assumption that has broken in every prior airline cycle.

**New voices, same script.** Toby Enqvist replaced Brett Hart on operations in Q2 2025 and delivered the Newark section without deviation. Glen Hauenstein's retirement (Q4 2025) drew a warm tribute from Kirby that doubled as a competitive note: *"your retirement timing is impeccable."* No dissent has entered the room.

**The Chase renewal is being pre-negotiated in public.** Q1 2026: *"the details regarding our deal with Chase are largely confidential, but I think you can Google the expiration date and know that it's not tomorrow, but it's not that far off."* Nocella is signalling to Chase, through the market, that United has leverage — record cardholder penetration, "incredible" spend uplift. This is the most valuable undated event in the file and nobody on the call pressed him on it.

**The Spirit answer reveals the real capacity risk.** Kirby, Q1 2026, on a potential Spirit bailout: *"I don't think this crisis is anywhere near big enough to cause the need for an airline bail out."* He is arguing *against* a competitor's rescue. If the administration bails Spirit out, capacity that United's entire pricing bridge assumes will exit, does not exit.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.** Not a close call on the business, and not the same question as whether to buy the stock. United grew earnings through a year in which a quarter of its cost base doubled, beat eight of eight quarters, recovered half a fuel shock inside one quarter, is tracking fourth-quarter yields up 19%, and gave up its own guidance sandbag in the same breath. The franchise is better than it was three years ago and the direction is real.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing: this is not an airline position, it is a levered short position in the price of crude oil, wearing a quality-franchise costume.**

Every load-bearing element of the case resolves on one variable United does not control. The 2027 double-digit margin target requires 100% fuel pass-through. The $9–$11 guide is struck on a specific curve — management quantified the sensitivity themselves: *"The fuel price spike this month is equal to $1.12 of EPS."* That is roughly 11% of the guide midpoint, from one month of one commodity. Brent is $84.82 today against roughly $71 on July 1 — up about 19% in sixteen days on renewed strikes around Hormuz. The 60-day ceasefire clock signed on June 17 runs out around mid-August.

So the director is being asked to underwrite a franchise thesis and will be paid or punished by a war. The quality of the eight-quarter execution record does not reduce that exposure by one basis point. Size it as an oil position, not as a compounder, and do not let the (deserved) admiration for the operating record smuggle in a risk you did not intend to take.

**Economic moat: NARROW.**

The moat type is real and it is a blend: **regulatory-license** (hub gates and slots, and specifically the FAA hourly caps at Newark — an awarded, durable advantage), **intangible-brand plus switching-costs** (MileagePlus and the Chase co-brand, where the flywheel is corroborated by record cardholder penetration and 22% account growth through a fare shock), and **scale-cost** at seven hubs.

But the evidence forbids calling it wide. **Return on invested capital is 4.3%** — below any plausible cost of capital. Return on equity is 9.3%. Net margin is 5.7% and sits 0.37 standard deviations *below* its own historical peak. A moat is measured in returns on capital, not in market share, and United's returns say it has bought share with capital rather than extracted rent from a position. Gross margin at 64.1% and expanding is a favourable data point; it has not reached the bottom line.

**Moat trend: WIDENING.** Direction and level disagree here, and the honest answer records both. The level is poor; the trend is genuinely favourable, and on evidence rather than narrative: earnings per share from −$6.10 in 2021 to $10.22 in 2025; book value per share compounding about 31.5% a year over five years; premium unit revenue leading the main cabin by 4 points for two consecutive quarters; loyalty penetration at record levels; the Newark caps awarded and permanent; and the competitive field thinning as low-cost carriers retreat from expensive hubs and Spirit fails. This is a narrow moat getting wider, not a wide moat eroding. The distinction matters for sizing: it argues against treating the low multiple as a trap, and equally against paying a quality multiple for a 4.3% return.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE. No secular decline theme applies.**

Nothing in the file threatens the terminal value of air travel. Videoconferencing was supposed to kill business travel and business ticketed revenue was up 14% year over year in Q1 2026. Artificial intelligence does not displace the product; it lowers United's own cost to deliver it — Kirby's technology programme is a cost tailwind, not a disruption. Channel shift has already happened and United won it (86% day-of app usage). The energy transition is a long-dated cost pressure on a hard-to-abate sector, but there is no evidence in the record of it impairing terminal value on any horizon that matters, and no honest secular-decline label fits this name.

**The threat here is cyclical and it is severe — but severe and cyclical is not the same as terminal.** Fuel, war, recession and the industry's chronic inability to hold pricing discipline through a delivery ramp are real and they are why the multiple is low. They are not structural erosion of the earnings base.

**Therefore: the cheapness is neither a fear-print nor a value trap. It is an accurate price for a cyclical.** This is the finding the director most needs, because both easy answers are wrong. The base is not shrinking, so this is not a trap — the trap label requires a melting terminal value and there is none. But the low multiple is not a mispricing either: at 4.3% returns on invested capital, an Altman-Z of 1.2, free cash flow down 33%, peak capital spending still ahead, and every forward promise hostage to Brent crude, roughly seven times out-year earnings is approximately what this asset is worth. The market is not scared of United. The market is correctly pricing an improving franchise that does not yet earn its cost of capital and cannot control its largest input.

One further caution on the screen that surfaced this name. It carries a 75% margin of safety, and that number is an artifact. Four of five valuation methods fail outright — discounted cash flow, earnings power value, owner-earnings and a fifteen-times-earnings check all return invalid or deeply negative readings, because free cash flow does not cover them. Only the Graham revised formula produces a positive reading, and it does so by capitalising a cyclical peak earnings figure against a +44% forward growth input. That is the exact recipe that generates false bargains in cyclicals at the top of their earnings cycle. The two surviving models disagree by a factor of 4.6 — a discounted-cash-flow value of $45.80 against a Buffett-style value of $212.06. When the models disagree that violently, they are not measuring value; they are measuring their own assumptions. Do not let the 75% into the sizing discussion.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 4 | TRAJECTORY: STRENGTHENING | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: WIDENING | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable

bull_thesis:
United has spent a decade building something the market still prices as a commodity airline, and the last four quarters are the proof it wanted. The core claim, repeated on every call since early 2025, is that United has won the customers who choose an airline by name rather than by price, and that this win is durable. Unusually for a management slogan, the hard numbers corroborate it. In the second quarter of 2026, reported on July 15, revenue rose 16% to $17.67B and adjusted earnings came in at $1.99 a share, the top of management's own $1-to-$2 guide and ahead of the roughly $1.91 the street expected. That was the eighth consecutive quarterly beat. It was delivered while absorbing a $2.3B year-over-year increase in the fuel bill, and United still posted a 4.8% pretax margin.

The engine underneath is the loyalty business, and it is the part the market undervalues most. New co-branded credit card accounts hit a record for a second quarter, up 22%, with card spend up 14% and MileagePlus enrollments up 9% - outpacing capacity growth by 5 points - all during a quarter when fares were rising sharply. Premium revenue rose 16.4% with premium unit revenue up 11.6%, leading the main cabin. This is a capital-light, contracted, annuity-like cash stream sitting inside a business the market values as if it were only metal and jet fuel. Management flagged the potential to double the loyalty program's earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) back in the third quarter of 2025, and the Chase co-brand agreement comes up for renewal on a timeline management hinted is 'not that far off' - a renegotiation United enters with record cardholder penetration as leverage.

The pricing evidence is the freshest and strongest leg. United recovered about half of the fuel increase within a single quarter. Fourth-quarter yields are currently tracking up 19% year over year, against Q3 yields that were up only 5% at the same point in the booking curve, with selling yields up mid-to-high teens in recent weeks. Management's stated bridge - yields need to rise about 15-20% to recover 100% of the fuel cost - is visibly being crossed in real time. Critically, the demand destruction that Kirby himself predicted in April 2026 ('ECON 101 makes us believe it's coming') has not appeared across two quarters of sharply higher fares. United set passenger records anyway. If the brand-loyalty thesis is right, that is exactly what it should look like.

The structural backdrop is genuinely improving and not by United's own telling. Low-cost carriers are retreating from expensive hubs, Spirit's business model is failing, and unprofitable capacity is leaving the system. United's Newark hub emerged from its 2025 crisis with FAA hourly flight caps - an awarded, durable regulatory advantage competitors cannot easily lobby away. Engines, not airframes, cap industry growth, which limits the classic airline sin of flooding capacity into a recovery. Management targets double-digit pretax margins in 2027 and mid-teens beyond, with confidence that 'has never been higher,' plus free cash flow conversion of 50% near-term rising to 75% by the end of the decade and net debt below two turns of earnings on the way to an investment-grade rating.

Valuation is the kicker. At $118.81, United trades at roughly 6.9 times the $17.32 of 2028 consensus earnings, against Delta at about 8.6 times the same-year consensus - a 20% discount to a peer with a worse growth profile. Kirby's own framing on the July 16 call: 'our multiples do not yet reflect it, we believe this industry has structurally changed.' Management also quantified how much of the current gloom is one month of oil: 'The fuel price spike this month is equal to $1.12 of EPS. So if you will go back to where it was earlier this month, we expect to be above the high end of the guidance range.'

Conditions that must hold: crude retreats from today's $84.82 Brent toward the $70 area, or United completes 100% pass-through without the elasticity shoe dropping; competitors hold pricing discipline through an 8% fleet growth year; the Chase renewal lands at improved economics; capital spending peaks and free cash flow conversion turns; and the 2027 double-digit pretax margin actually arrives on schedule rather than slipping a third time.

Net margin is 5.7%, sitting 0.37 standard deviations below its own historical peak. A company that has 'won' its market and still earns 4.3% on capital has won share, not economics - it bought the share with shareholders' money. Six quarters of describing the change as 'structural, permanent and irreversible' has not moved returns on capital at all, and airlines have declared structural change before every cycle in living memory.

Management's one testable forward promise has already failed. Leskinen said in the second quarter of 2025 that he 'fully expect[s] free cash flow to expand' and 'free cash flow conversion to expand both.' Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is $2.54B, down 33% year over year. Asked directly in July 2026 when capital spending peaks, he gave a conversion ratio instead of a year, then added the escape hatch: 'As we get there faster, we may allow CapEx to be a little bit higher.' The Altman-Z solvency score of 1.2 sits in the distress zone, carried into a doubled-fuel environment against $17.03B of net debt including capitalised leases ($9.83B excluding them).

The margin promise is a moving target with a perfect track record of moving. 'At least 1 point or more of margin each year' (October 2025) produced net margins of 5.5%, 5.5%, 5.7% across 2023-2025 - flat. Wolfe's Scott Group caught this in January 2026 and got a compliment ('I love that you did the math') instead of a date. By April 2026 double-digit margins were 'next year,' meaning 2027. Each restatement arrives with more stated confidence and less near-term visibility. Two quarters later he has not revisited his own forecast and nobody has made him. Fourth-quarter yields tracking up 19% is not margin expansion - it is cost neutralisation, passing a doubled input through to a customer who has not yet said no. The bear case is simply that the textbook is right and merely lagged, landing in a quarter nobody has modelled, while the fleet grows 8%.

The pricing thesis also assumes competitors behave - the assumption that has broken in every prior airline cycle. Management is already reframing this: 'the cost structure inflation and the harmonies that mean everyone's costs have gone up... it is 90% of the driver.' That is groundwork for arguing fares must rise industry-wide. But if the administration bails out Spirit - which Kirby argued against in April 2026 - the capacity United's entire pricing bridge assumes will exit does not exit.

What confirms the bear: Brent holding above $85 through the mid-August ceasefire expiry; the October 21 third-quarter print showing unit revenue decelerating as elasticity bites; the 2027 double-digit margin target slipping a third time; or a Spirit rescue that keeps unprofitable seats in the market.
consensus_delta:
The street is wrong about United, but not in the direction a buyer would need. The disagreement is about what the pricing data means, not whether it is real.

The average analyst target of $154.70 (median $157.50, high $190 set by Morgan Stanley's Ravi Shanker on 2026-07-16, low $112) requires United to earn something near $16-$18 and hold a 9-10x multiple. The whole street is treating fuel recovery as a question of timing rather than level. That is the error. Recovering 100% of a doubled fuel cost does not restore the prior margin structure - it restores the prior margin on a much larger revenue base, which is a lower margin percentage, and it takes the entire 15-20% yield increase just to stand still.

Here is the sharpest delta, and it cuts against the bulls: the street is modelling 'Q4 yields tracking up 19% year over year' as revenue upside. It is not upside. It is cost neutralisation - passing a doubled input through to a customer who has not yet said no. Every dollar of that 19% is spoken for by fuel before it reaches an operating margin. The 19% is a genuinely impressive datapoint about United's pricing power and a genuinely misleading one about United's earnings power, and the street has booked it as the latter.

Second delta: the July 15 'guidance raise' is being read as an increase when it is a narrowing. The range went from $7-to-$11 to $9-to-$11. The ceiling did not move even as nearly $6B of fuel cost was disclosed - only the floor lifted. The midpoint of $10 is about 6% below 2025's roughly $10.66. Headlines read 'lifts outlook.' The arithmetic reads 'flat-to-down year, narrower range.' First-half earnings of $3.18 are down a third from about $4.78.

Third delta, and this one is where the street is too bearish: the Q3 guide of $2.50-to-$3.50 against roughly $3.60 consensus is NOT a demand miss and is being punished as one. It is an accounting-policy change. On 2026-07-16 management said: 'we have decided to once again be a leader by changing our guidance policy on fuel... provide guidance to reflect the most current fuel prices,' striking the guide at about $3.69 a gallon on Tuesday's curve. United gave up its own sandbag - the sandbag that produced eight consecutive beats - and the street marked the resulting honest number down as a deterioration. That is a real misread, and it is why the name deserves a hearing rather than a dismissal.

But here is why none of it becomes a buy. All three deltas cancel to approximately the current price. The street's $155 is too high because it books cost-recovery as upside. The street's Q3 disappointment is too harsh because it misreads a policy change as a miss. Net the two errors and United is worth roughly $125 - about 5% above the $118.81 tape. Being right about both of Wall Street's mistakes earns nothing here.

On the screen's framing for a deep-value name - is the market pricing terminal decline into stable or growing earnings power? No, and that is the answer that closes the case. There is no terminal decline priced in. At roughly 6.9x 2028 consensus earnings against Delta's 8.6x, the market is pricing a cyclical with a 4.3% return on invested capital, an Altman-Z solvency score of 1.2, and total exposure to one commodity - approximately correctly. The 75% margin of safety on the screen is an artifact and must not enter the sizing discussion: four of five valuation methods fail outright (discounted cash flow, earnings power value, owner-earnings and a fifteen-times-earnings check all return invalid or deeply negative), and only the Graham revised formula produces a positive reading, by capitalising cyclical peak earnings against a +44.3% forward growth input. The two surviving models disagree by a factor of 4.6 - $45.80 versus $212.06. That is not a valuation range; it is two models with no idea, and the screen averaged their confusion into a bargain.
forcing_function:
There is no adequate one, and this is the finding that decides the verdict rather than a footnote to it.

The load-bearing catalyst already fired. United reported the second quarter on 2026-07-15 after the close: adjusted earnings of $1.99 versus about $1.91 expected, revenue of $17.67B versus about $17.60B, the full-year guide narrowed to $9-to-$11 from $7-to-$11, and the Q3 guide set at $2.50-to-$3.50 against roughly $3.60 consensus. The call followed on 2026-07-16. The market's answer was a decline to $118.81, extending a roughly 12% fall from about $135 on July 7. The event happened, the re-rate is spent, and it went the wrong way. This is not an asymmetric special situation; it is a post-event cyclical.

What remains is soft, and every piece of it is undated, non-binding, or someone else's decision:
- The 2027 double-digit pretax margin target is a management aspiration with no binding date. It has now been restated three times - 'at least 1 point or more of margin each year' (October 2025) delivered flat margins of 5.5%, 5.5%, 5.7% across 2023-2025; then double-digit 'next year' (April 2026); now 'confidence... has never been higher' (July 2026). A target that keeps moving is not a forcing function.
- An investment-grade upgrade is a rating-agency decision, undated, third-party. Leskinen said only that 'we have had significant consultations with the rating agencies' and plans for net debt below two turns.
- The Chase co-brand renewal is the most genuinely valuable undated event in the file and the one thing that could crystallise the loyalty value the base case assigns $67 a share to. Nocella in April 2026: 'the details regarding our deal with Chase are largely confidential, but I think you can Google the expiration date and know that it's not tomorrow, but it's not that far off.' No date. Not underwritable.
- Consolidation rumours, which Kirby pre-emptively refused to discuss in April 2026. Unverified and unverifiable.
- Third-quarter earnings on 2026-10-21 is the only hard date. It is a routine print, not a re-rating event - and given the new fuel policy marks guidance to the live curve, it is now a *harder* bar, not a spring-loaded one.

The only thing that actually re-rates this stock is the price of crude oil, and the nearest dated instance of it - the US-Iran ceasefire clock expiring around mid-August - is a risk, not a catalyst. It is also a macro binary United does not control, cannot hedge in the eyes of an equity holder, and shares with every other airline.

On the deep-value screen's own framing - what event forces the market to re-rate: a buyback authorisation, an activist, an asset sale, a dividend initiation? None are present. There is no buyback discussion on the July 16 call. There is no activist. There is no asset sale. There is no dividend. The sum-of-the-parts discount is modest (about 5%) and there is no mechanism to close it and no one pushing.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months are where this thesis gets tested, and United enters the window with no cushion and no control over the variable that decides it.

The fuel curve is the whole risk. Brent is $84.82 today (West Texas Intermediate $79.50) against roughly $71 on July 1 - up about 19% in sixteen days on renewed US-Iran strikes around the Strait of Hormuz. Management sized the sensitivity themselves on July 16: 'The fuel price spike this month is equal to $1.12 of EPS.' That is about 11% of the $10 guide midpoint from one month of one commodity. The Q3 guide of $2.50-to-$3.50 is struck at an all-in fuel price of about $3.69 a gallon on 'Tuesday's curve' - which means it is already stale, and it breaks if crude keeps climbing.

The dated event that matters is not United's. The 60-day US-Iran ceasefire signed on June 17 expires around mid-August. That clock, not the October earnings print, is what sets the fourth-quarter fuel line and therefore the fourth quarter's implied $3.32-to-$4.32 of earnings per share - a number that must rise from $3.10 in the prior-year quarter to make the full-year guide work, and which depends entirely on those Q4 yields tracking up 19% actually converting. If crude breaks higher into the expiry, the guide that was just 'raised' gets cut inside a quarter.

The elasticity shoe is the second hazard and it is unmodelled. Kirby predicted in April 2026 that a 15-20% yield increase must reduce demand: 'While we haven't actually seen that decline yet, ECON 101 makes us believe it's coming.' Two quarters later it has not come and he has not revisited the forecast. But United is pushing fourth-quarter yields up 19% while growing the fleet about 8%. If the textbook is merely lagged rather than wrong, it lands in Q4 2026 or Q1 2027 - inside this window - and it lands on top of elevated fuel. That combination is not in anyone's model, including the $190 target set yesterday.

The balance sheet offers no shock absorber. Free cash flow is $2.54B on a trailing basis, down 33% year over year, with peak capital spending still ahead - management would not name a peak year when asked directly on July 16, offering a 50% conversion ratio instead and the caveat 'we may allow CapEx to be a little bit higher.' Net debt is $17.03B including capitalised leases ($9.83B excluding). The Altman-Z solvency score of 1.2 sits in the distress zone. Liquidity is genuinely strong at $16.64B of cash and short-term investments - United will not have a financing problem in this window. But it has no room to absorb a fuel shock and a demand shock together without the investment-grade goal and the sub-two-turns leverage target both slipping.

A third, quieter risk: a Spirit rescue. Kirby argued against one in April 2026 ('I don't think this crisis is anywhere near big enough to cause the need for an airline bail out'), which tells you he understands the stakes. United's entire pricing bridge assumes unprofitable capacity keeps exiting. A government bailout keeps those seats in the market precisely when United is asking customers to pay 19% more.

The forecastable sequence: crude stays elevated through the mid-August ceasefire expiry; the October 21 print shows the fuel pass-through decelerating or unit revenue softening as elasticity arrives; the 2027 double-digit margin target slips a third time. None of that is a solvency event. All of it is a $75-to-$95 stock.
positioning_washout:
There is no washout coming, and that is precisely the problem - it removes the only entry this setup could justify.

United has no dividend and therefore no yield-focused shareholder base to be mechanically forced out by a cut. There is no pivot, no distribution change, no index event, no spin, no forced-seller mechanic of any kind in this name. Institutional flow scores a neutral 50/100 and smart-money 62/100 - engaged, not crowded, not fleeing. Nothing here liquidates on a rule.

What actually moves the stock is discretionary de-grossing of oil beta, and it is orderly rather than mechanical. The evidence is clean: on July 8, American fell 5%, United 4%, and Delta and JetBlue 3% - together, on crude. Books do not dump United; they reduce airline exposure as a group when oil moves. That produces correlated drawdowns without the price-insensitive, forced dislocation that creates genuine entry points.

The recent price action is a momentum unwind, not capitulation. United ran from a 52-week low of $82.42 to a high of $138.77, sat about $135 on July 7, and is $118.81 today - down roughly 12% in ten days. It still trades about 16% above its 200-day average and 68% up its 52-week range, above both its 50-day ($112.57) and 200-day ($104.24) averages. Nobody is capitulating. Holders are trimming a winner into an oil headline. A name 16% above its 200-day average with a 100% beat rate does not have a washed-out shareholder base - it has a satisfied one.

The one genuinely informative flow signal points the wrong way for bulls, and it is the insiders. Zero open-market purchases against five sales totalling 96,381 shares. Set that against Kirby's July 16 line - 'our multiples do not yet reflect it, we believe this industry has structurally changed.' Management is arguing publicly that the market undervalues United while privately selling into that market. The grant-inflated buy ratio on the screen reads 0.00 for a reason.

The conclusion for timing: a name whose only re-rating path is an oil price, with no forced seller to create the entry and no floor beneath it, offers no structural moment to buy. If a mid-August ceasefire failure spikes crude and takes United toward the $85-$95 region on genuine sector-wide de-grossing, that would be a real dislocation - and at that price, against a $125 base-case fair value and a $175 favorable case, the risk-reward inverts and the committee should be interested. That is the specific event to wait for. It has not happened, and today's 12% pullback is not it.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now - at this price, not on this business. The distinction matters, because the temptation here is to be wrong in the flattering direction.

Start with what is real, because a lot of it is. United grew earnings through a year in which a quarter of its cost base doubled. It has beaten eight of eight quarters. It recovered about half of a $2.3B fuel shock inside a single quarter and still posted a 4.8% pretax margin. Fourth-quarter yields are tracking up 19% year over year. The loyalty flywheel grew through a fare shock - record second-quarter co-brand accounts up 22%, card spend up 14%. The Newark hourly flight caps are a genuine, awarded regulatory advantage. And on 2026-07-16 management voluntarily surrendered the sandbag that produced its own beat streak, marking guidance to the live fuel curve because 'we feel we owe it to investors.' That is a rare and creditable act, and the street punished it by reading an honest number as a miss. Credibility here scores a 4 out of 5, the trajectory is genuinely strengthening, and this is a better franchise than it was three years ago. None of that is in dispute.

The problem is that being right about all of it earns about 5%.

Two independent methods land in the same place. Valuing the business by its parts on normalised 2027 earnings - the loyalty annuity at 9x for about $67 a share, cargo at $6, core flying at 4.25x for about $109, less $52 a share of net debt including capitalised leases - gives about $128. Cross-checking against the peer anchor pulled live today - Delta at about 8.6x same-vintage consensus, applied to a base-case 2027 figure near $14 - gives about $119. Call it $125. The stock is $118.81. There is no discount here to harvest. The screen's 75% margin of safety is an artifact of a single surviving model capitalising cyclical peak earnings against a +44.3% growth input while four other methods fail outright, and the two survivors disagree by a factor of 4.6 ($45.80 against $212.06). That is not a valuation; it is noise averaged into a bargain.

The regime settles it. The current read is explicit that the fattest lanes are structural special situations in thin-coverage names, and that theses hinging on one shared macro factor - it names oil specifically - must be penalised on resolution-driver independence. United fails on every axis. It is one of the most heavily covered equities in the market (38 price targets in the past year), so there is no coverage edge. It is not a special situation - no spin, no forced seller, no activist, no deal. And its entire forward case resolves on Brent crude, which management itself sized at $1.12 of earnings per share for one month's move - about 11% of the guide midpoint. Worse, the regime document's own oil tripwire is breaching underneath it: it recorded 'NOT BREACHED' at Brent $71.20 on July 1; Brent is $84.82 today, up about 19% in sixteen days on renewed Hormuz strikes, with the 60-day ceasefire signed June 17 expiring around mid-August. The playbook for that breach says de-risk oil-sensitive names mid-event. United is the definition of oil-sensitive, mid-event.

And the catalyst is spent. The second-quarter print landed on July 15 and the re-rate went the wrong way - the stock is down roughly 12% from about $135 on July 7. What is left is a 2027 margin target that has already slipped twice, an undated rating-agency decision, an undated Chase renewal, and a routine October 21 print that the new fuel policy has made harder rather than spring-loaded. The only thing that genuinely re-rates this stock is a commodity price, and the nearest dated instance of it is a risk rather than a catalyst.

So the arithmetic: about 37% downside to an adverse case of $75, about 5% upside to fair value, no structural floor beneath it - no deal terms, no net cash (this is $17.03B of net debt), no tender. The 52-week low of $82.42 is a chart level, not protection. Roughly seven units of risk per unit of reward, where the reward needs both the 2027 earnings and a multiple re-rating to arrive together and the risk needs only for oil to stay exactly where it already is.

On the value case judged alone - ignoring the spent catalyst and the regime entirely - the answer is the same and for an unrelated reason. A 5% discount to fair value is not a value case, however good the forensics. And the returns forbid paying up: a 4.3% return on invested capital is below any plausible cost of capital, which means six quarters of 'structural, permanent and irreversible' have bought market share with shareholders' money rather than earned rent from a position. The moat is real but narrow - hub slots, the Newark caps, the MileagePlus and Chase switching costs - and it is genuinely widening, which is why this is not a value trap: the earnings base is not melting, no secular force threatens air travel's terminal value, and the low multiple is therefore accurate rather than fearful. The market is not scared of United. It is correctly pricing an improving franchise that does not yet earn its cost of capital and cannot control its largest input. Both easy answers - hidden gem, value trap - are wrong, and the boring middle is the truth.

One last tell. Kirby argues publicly that 'our multiples do not yet reflect it.' Insiders have made zero open-market purchases against five sales totalling 96,381 shares. When management tells the market it is undervalued and sells into that market, believe the trades.

What would change this. There is no washout to wait for in the ordinary sense - no dividend to cut, no index event, no forced seller; airline books de-gross discretionarily and orderly, which is why the current 12% pullback is a momentum unwind and not an opportunity. But a genuine dislocation is identifiable: a mid-August ceasefire failure that spikes crude and drags the whole sector down would take United toward $85-$95 on price-insensitive sector-wide de-grossing. At that price, against a $125 base and a $175 favorable case, the risk-reward inverts and this committee should be actively interested - the franchise quality is real and would then be available at a price that pays for the oil exposure. Watch it, keep the work current, and do not confuse admiration for the operating record with a reason to own the stock at $118.81.
